city.record_kind: the official long-term record NOAA keeps for the city, joining several sites over the years
city.caveat: This is the official city record as kept, without adjustments. It joins several observing sites over the years, and a move, a new instrument or the city growing around a station can shift readings (city growth mostly warms nights); NOAA's adjusted climate datasets correct for these. Treat any single number as approximate.

text.lede: Yesterday's high of 52°F was typical for November 13.
text.p_yest: The high of 52°F was typical for November 13. The normal high for the date is 58°F, and the record is 80°F (1879). The low of 41°F was typical for November 13.
text.t_rec: Washington has nearly stopped setting record lows
text.p_rec: If Washington's climate weren't changing, every year would have the same chance of holding a daily record. Since 2000, Washington has set 3 standing record lows, far fewer than the 63 that chance alone would give, and 87 record highs, more than the 63 that chance alone would give. The 1990s hold the most record highs of any decade (37). Washington's all-time high is 106°F, on August 6, 1918.
text.t_chg: Washington's days and nights both warmed. Nights warmed faster.
text.p_chg: Across 154 complete years: Washington's average low has risen +0.40°F per decade (95% range +0.36 to +0.44), about +6.2°F since 1872. Washington's average high has risen +0.31°F per decade (95% range +0.27 to +0.36), about +4.8°F since 1872.
text.t_mon: Lows rose in all 12 months. Highs rose in all 12 months.
text.t_rain: Rain and snow: no clear long-term change
text.p_rain: Washington's yearly precipitation shows no clear long-term change (−0.16 inches per decade, a range that includes zero). The 1991–2020 normal is 41.8 inches a year. The wettest year was 2018 (66.28 in); the driest, 1930 (21.66 in).
